 if (a < b) {
 return b;
 }
 int diff = a - b;
 return foo(diff, b - 1) + foo(diff, b + 1);
}

Which one of the following statements best describes the function fooin the above code?

options.text: Causes a runtime error because functions in C cannot be recursive.
The function <code>foo</code>is an example of an iterative method.
The value of <code>diff</code> is shared across all recursive calls.
Each recursive call to <code>foo</code> has its own local, temporary variable <code>diff</code>.

}

{

 y = 2;

 swap(&x, &y, &z);
 printf("x = %d y = %d z = %d\n", x, y, z);

questions.qtext:
The following C program compiles and runs without errors. What is the output?

#include<stdio.h>
void swap(int count, int A[], int B[])
{
 int i, temp;
 for (i = 0; i < count; ++i)
 {
 temp = A[i];
 A[i] = B[i];
 B[i] = temp;
 }
}
int main(void)
{
 int A[5] = {1, 6, 4, 5, 9};
 int B[5] = {2, 7, 11, 14, 3};
 int C[7] = {1, 8, 15, 22, 29, 2, 9};
 swap(3, A, B);
 swap(4, B, C);
 swap(5, A, C);
 printf("%d %d %d\n", A[3], B[4], C[5]);
 return;
}

questions.qtext:
Which of the following loops produces the same value for the variable x as the loop shown below?
 

int i, x = 0;
for(i = 0; i <= 100; ++i)
 x += i;
printf("x = %d \n", x); /* prints x = 5050 */

options.text:
int i = 0, x = 0;
while (i <= 100)
 x += i;
printf("x = %d\n", x);

int i = 0, x = 0;
do {
 x += i;
} while (i <= 100);
++i;
printf("x = %d\n", x);

int i = 0, x = 0;
while (i <= 100) {
 x += i++;
}
printf("x = %d\n", x);

int i = 0, x = 0;
while (i <= 100) {
 x += ++i;
}
printf("x = %d\n", x);
